newsitem.title: India: India coalition ponders new political deal.
newsitem.headline: India coalition ponders new political deal.

text.p: India's defeated coalition showed signs of considering a deal with its Congress party ally-turned-foe on Saturday to find a new government after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was toppled in a confidence vote.

A close aide of a key political negotiator in Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front told Reuters that the alliance had in its internal talks shown a willingness to consider replacing its leader to make peace with the Congress party.
"There is no other way," the aide, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters as the decision-making Steering Committee of the centre-left United Front held a meeting.

Deve Gowda resigned on Friday when his coalition was defeated in parliament in a confidence vote after the Congress withdrew vital support and refused to resume backing his alliance unless it changed its leader.

The alliance has so far refused to yield. "There is complete unity and, what is more there is complete unanimity -- there is no question of a change in leadership," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told a news conference.
Sensing a widespread move among lawmakers to avoid fresh elections, leaders sought to form a new coalition, but the United Front said it was not afraid of a snap poll.
"Nobody is itching to go to the polls. But if it becomes inevitable, we will not shy away from the polls," Reddy said.
The defeated government was formed last June by the alliance, which has 178 lawmakers, with support from the Congress, which has 140 deputies in the 545-member lower house.

They closed ranks last year to oust a 12-day-old government formed by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Jnnata Party (BJP), which controls 193 deputies. The groups accuse the BJP of favouring majority Hindus over India's Moslem minority.
President Shankar Dayal Sharma has asked Deve Gowda to remain as caretaker prime minister while efforts are made to forge a new governing majority in the hung parliament.
The front was still weighing its options, and there were differences within the coalition, the aide said.
"Deve Gowda says they (the alliance) can do well in an election. But there are others in the United Front who do not want a mid-term poll," he said.
As a last effort to avert a mid-term poll, a change of leadership could be considered, he said.

"I don't see any rhyme or reason for the Congress decision to withdraw support to the government. So we have no other way out but to go for the mandate of the people," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Deve Gowda as saying in a television report.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri accused Deve Gowda of not containing the BJP when he withdrew his party's support to him, but is widely seen as having made a personal bid for power.
The Congress party, keen to sidestep early elections, said on Saturday it had no plans to seek power and reiterated it would support the United Front if it replaced Deve Gowda.
But signs of a leadership tussle appeared within its own ranks, following Kesri's accusations of Deve Gowda widely described as whimsical and unsubstantiated.

More than 100 Congress lawmakers met on Saturday to speak against Kesri's call to vote out Deve Gowda, which they obeyed under protest, a lawmaker said, adding that there were some demands that a Congress leader, Sharad Pawar, challenge Kesri for the leadership.
"Everybody was very anguished at yesterday's debacle," he said, referring to the debate on the vote.
The decision-making Congress Working Committee was scheduled to meet on Monday and its parliamentary group on April 20.
A senior United Front official said: "The Congress is undergoing cataclysmic convulsions. We are watching the health of the Congress party and getting periodic health bulletins."
